content:
The moderators over at MathOverflow are considering updating their AI generated content policy. (Currently the official policy is that all AI generated content "will likely be deleted".) I raised the issue of autoformalization, because I had been unable to generate an argument for why you would ban AI-generated Lean code.

It turns out I was insufficiently creative: you could just ban Lean entirely. A moderator says that "I personally don't think it's worth actually posting Lean code here" and further asks "How are non-Lean-speakers supposed to vote on an answer, even on a topic they are experts in, if they can't parse it?"

https://meta.mathoverflow.net/questions/6423/possible-updates-to-our-ai-generated-content-policy

For the sake of clarity, that moderator was me. I gave the example of an answer just being pasting Mathematica code. The defacto official language of the site is English, and pasting chunks of Lean is not as useful for the vast majority of mathematicians, who would hope for an answer that explains why the thing is true.

I said to Boris that one can (in my view) link to Lean code off-site, as part of an answer that gives a human-written answer in ordinary mathematical prose that explains the answer in a self-contained way.

MO is for people to ask questions, and if the answer is not something they can understand, that's not useful to them. One might ask people to learn Lean, but then one might as well demand people learn French or German to understand someone's answer.
I hope that people appreciate that I am not anti-Lean, since I hang out here to keep myself informed. I also use AI in my day job for coding tasks.

BTW, there has been at least one person in the past week or so who posted a links to their crank preprint that came with a library of over a hundred LLM-generated Lean files. It wasn't worth the paper it wasn't even written on. Obviously the human operator needs to verify and publicly certify that the definitions and theorem statements are correctly formalised at minimum

Those who aren't regular MathOverflow users might lack some of the context to understand Boris Alexeev's comments, so let me try to supply some of that context.

The proposal is for MO to become more permissive about AI-generated content (Lean or otherwise), not less permissive, let alone start banning things that weren't banned before. Until Boris brought it up, Lean wasn't even specifically part of the conversation. I can't recall ever seeing anyone post Lean code on MO (though I wouldn't be shocked if it has happened, since even though I'm a pretty heavy MO user, I view only a tiny fraction of the content there). David Roberts was by no means suggesting that MO suddenly start banning Lean, but just questioning whether posting Lean to MO makes sense. Certainly I don't see why AI-generated Lean would be more suitable for MO than human-generated Lean would be. But in any case, the appropriateness of posting Lean to MO is really an orthogonal question to the question of whether to relax the near-ban on AI-generated content. And just to be clear, if the new proposal is approved, it would if anything make MO more accepting of AI-generated Lean than it has been so far, so I don't see any reason for Lean fans to get upset.

Also for what it's worth, I kind of agree with David Roberts's opinion (which he said was a personal opinion and not a moderator policy) that posting Lean code to MO would rarely improve an MO answer (or question). People sometimes post Python code or Mathematica code or whatever, which one could argue is helpful for someone who wants to reproduce a particular computation, but I personally find such answers slightly annoying because they clutter up the page. In most such cases, I think people would do well to follow David Roberts's suggestion to post the code off-site and point people to it.

Timothy Chow said:

I can't recall ever seeing anyone post Lean code on MO (though I wouldn't be shocked if it has happened, since even though I'm a pretty heavy MO user, I view only a tiny fraction of the content there).

As I mention in my comment on meta.MO, one significant reason there hasn't been much Lean code posted on the site is because the official policy bans AI-generated content.

I posted an answer 2 days ago that included a Lean formalization. (When I include Lean code anywhere, I usually link the words "Type-check it online!" to "Lean 4 Web", not paste the code inline.) My friend Vipul Naik posted an answer 2 months ago that includes a Lean formalization. All of the content of both of these answers was AI-generated, so they violate site policy.

I have other Lean formalizations of solutions to MathOverflow problems. Some are unanswered questions. One improves a result from "a constant exists" to "here's an explicit constant". In one case where the formalization is of someone else's answer referencing a result in the literature, the published theorem is literally false (and I have a formal disproof), so the formalization also fixes the result itself. All of these Lean formalizations are AI-generated. I was aware that MO is very hostile to AI, so I do not plan to post any of these results on MO.

While I agree that the recent proposal is in the direction of being more permissive about AI-generated content, the new information to me was the current attitude towards Lean. I mentioned autoformalization because I was hoping for a carve-out in the policy for AI-generated Lean. It literally didn't occur to me that people might view even non-AI-generated Lean unfavorably. I think that the direct quote "How are non-Lean-speakers supposed to vote on an answer, even on a topic they are experts in, if they can't parse it?" speaks for itself, but I'm happy that David Roberts is here to express his point of view in detail himself.

Boris Alexeev said:

one significant reason there hasn't been much Lean code posted on the site is because the official policy bans AI-generated content.

citation needed. One reason I can think of is that most of the MO user base is not proficient in Lean, and those who are know that the rest can't necessarily make good use of such code.

I posted an answer 2 days ago that included a Lean formalization. (When I include Lean code anywhere, I usually link the words "Type-check it online!" to "Lean 4 Web", not paste the code inline.) My friend Vipul Naik posted an answer 2 months ago that includes a Lean formalization. All of the content of both of these answers was AI-generated, so they violate site policy.

Well, under the proposed policy this kind of answer would be ok, assuming you are willing to state that you believe it to be correct. [added: note also the non-anonymity is rather strong, including public identification; this bit was acknowledged to be possibly contentious in the private discussions before hand]

I'd like to also clarify that I thought you meant posting Lean on MathOverflow itself (as I hope was apparent by my reference to pasting Mathematica code), not giving a link in a longer answer written in the usual style (which is what I suggested would be more useful). Apologies for giving such a strong anti-Lean impression! I would be very happy if more people started posting good Lean formalisation of their answers, but this may not be universally popular, and also it's a slippery slope to people posting slop answers with "Lean formalisations" that are really misformalisations.

But enough about MO policy here. I would suggest making an answer at meta.mathoverflow under the announcement, making your case. I would probably upvote it.

Boris Alexeev said:

As I mention in my comment on meta.MO, one significant reason there hasn't been much Lean code posted on the site is because the official policy bans AI-generated content.

I don't understand this remark. Lean 3 has been around since 2017, long before AI-generated Lean was a thing. The ban cannot possibly explain the lack of Lean on MO from, say, 2017 to 2022.

@Boris Alexeev @Timothy Chow @David Michael Roberts I think this is a good discussion to have, but I've moved it to a new topic.
Lean on MO in 2018: https://mathoverflow.net/a/307239
(It's not a coincidence that my Zulip join-date is July 31, 2018.)
Note also the comments about dimension 8 and 24 sphere packing (only slightly later, in 2019)
@Johan Commelin thank you. I could tell it was taking up too much of the other thread, but I didn't want to leave the topic dangling

I think there are much better fora (even elsewhere on StackExchange) for AI proofs, especially when it gets to the point that a (slightly trained) human can tell whether a statement (and hopefully a proof) is correctly formalized. When enough of those proofs are presented elsewhere, they might be found and welcomed everywhere. The time for that has not yet come.

content:
Boris Alexeev said:

As I mention in my comment on meta.MO, one significant reason there hasn't been much Lean code posted on the site is because the official policy bans AI-generated content.

David Michael Roberts said:

citation needed

My message itself gives several examples of Lean content I am not allowed to post on MO.

Timothy Chow said:

I don't understand this remark. Lean 3 has been around since 2017, long before AI-generated Lean was a thing. The ban cannot possibly explain the lack of Lean on MO from, say, 2017 to 2022.

It seems pretty consistent to me:

  • Humans have not written very much Lean for MO, neither now nor before 2022.
  • AI is now able to generate Lean proofs of potential interest to MO, but this wasn't possible until recently. Moreover, AI can write Lean at a higher rate than a human.

Given that humans don't write much Lean for MO, the effect is: if AI is banned, there's almost no Lean at all, whereas if it's not banned, there is Lean. If humans did write for MO, the effect would still be similar: if AI is banned, there's some Lean, whereas if it's not banned, there is still much more Lean.

The formalization of solutions to Erdős problems offers concrete data regarding the alternate world:

  • Before 2022, no solutions were formalized.
  • Even by today, fewer than 10 solutions have been formalized by a human without AI.
  • But more than 100 solutions have been formalized using AI.

In other words, there is more than an order of magnitude more Lean formalization because AI is allowed.

I've heard many people express surprise that Erdős problems have received so much attention from AI. For example, Elliot Glazer suggests that solving highly upvoted problems on MO would be more exciting and of greater community interest.

But there's such a simple explanation for why there was so much activity around Erdős problems, and not interesting MathOverflow questions:

  • MathOverflow bans AI.
  • erdosproblems.com does not ban AI.

[Of course I have an opinion as to whether or not you should ban AI, but everything I'm saying here are purely "positive statements" (as opposed to "normative statements"). You can view this all the other way, as a way of preserving an artisanal human-centered craft community.]

In any case, the same is true for Lean: if you ban AI, you will get less Lean.

I think another reason Erdos problems get more lean attention is simply that lean can understand most interesting Erdos problems but it still can't understand most interesting MO questions because of missing definitions in mathlib

Kevin Buzzard said:

I think another reason Erdos problems get more lean attention is simply that lean can understand most interesting Erdos problems but it still can't understand most interesting MO questions because of missing definitions in mathlib

This extends to TCS. Successful uses of auto-formalization have so far been ones where the users used AI to prove pure math lemmas close to mathlib definitions and extrapolated from them with pen and paper.

@Boris Alexeev out of curiosity are you saying factually you personally didn't look at applying AI to MO questions in the past few years because of the ban? Or saying that in your opinion others don't do so because of it?

As described in my message above, I do apply AI to resolve MO questions. Just today, AI solved a problem from MathOverflow that I've wondered about since 2010. I just don't post the solutions, because I encounter so much hostility when I do: https://meta.mathoverflow.net/questions/6423/possible-updates-to-our-ai-generated-content-policy#comment35749_6423

That said, if AI weren't banned on MO, I feel confident I would have tried AI literally 10x more. And to be clear, usually the problems and solutions I would choose to work on would come with Lean (auto-)formalizations.

I am further very confident that other people would also try AI on MO questions. Lean auto-formalization would also play a significant role for other people, though not quite as often.
Boris, the whole point of the proposal is to make AI-generated answers not banned, going forward.

But, sadly, I have no more bandwidth to deal with this today, I've only managed to discuss it so in-depth because I've been off work, sick, and today I'm resuming (I'm not an academic, in case you didn't know).

Feel better! Thanks for coming here to express your viewpoints, and for moderating against the AI slop onslaught. Good luck with the AI policy.

Sadly: sorry a lot of this was a waste of time.

On a related note, my post on https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/ containing Lean code did not get deleted:
https://cstheory.stackexchange.com/questions/53222/semi-thue-systems-and-deterministic-computation
Was any of that Lean code AI-generated?

Timothy Chow said:

Was any of that Lean code AI-generated?

Asking about my post? Of course not!
I believe that's the point Tim is making.
Yes. If the Lean-code is human-generated, then of course there's no reason to ban it. The discussion initiated by Boris is whether AI-generated Lean code is appropriate on MathOverflow.

@Timothy Chow that seems like what in other fields is known as dissemination bias. I think those ideas could work for stack exchange since it it's based on puzzle solving, but users of that website are claiming its content is about research.

@René Perry please note that stackexchange and MathOverflow are different beasts. The latter is literally about research questions, the former is a generic Q&A platform, with all kinds of different cultures depending on the sub-site (puzzling, english language, cooking, coding, politics, ......)
